title: The Living Peoples
tagline: Ten Indigenous peoples alive today: their deep pasts, colonial dispossession and recovery of rights.
intro: Some peoples whose histories reach back thousands of years are living communities today. The ancestors of Aboriginal Australians reached Sahul 50,000 to 65,000 years ago, the Māori settled New Zealand around 1300, and the Lakota made the Black Hills their home by the 1770s. Most of these peoples met colonial rule, with killings, epidemics, forced removal and bans on their languages, and many have since won back land and recognition, from the Mabo Case in Australia to Nunavut and the Sámi parliaments. This path visits ten of them, in the order their histories begin.

steps.why: Their ancestors reached Sahul 50,000 to 65,000 years ago; more than 400 peoples, each with its own language and Country, survived British colonisation from 1788.
Descendants of hunter-gatherers who 10,000 years ago were spread from Tanzania to Cape Agulhas, the San faced a Dutch East India Company policy of eradication from 1777.
In the far north of Europe since the Bronze Age or early Iron Age, the Sámi bore centuries of assimilation and have elected parliaments of their own since Finland’s of 1973.
Herders of sheep and cattle since about the turn of the era, the Khoekhoe killed Francisco de Almeida at Salt River in 1510 and later lost their land to colonial conquest.
Amazigh herders and caravan traders of the Sahara with a founding queen, Tin Hinan, they resisted French conquest from 1881 to 1920 and saw their homeland divided among five states.
Descendants of the Thule people who spread east from the Bering Strait around 1000 CE, the Inuit survived forced relocation and won the land claim that created Nunavut in 1999.
The Indigenous people of Hokkaido, Sakhalin and the Kurils, whose culture took shape from the 13th century, lost land and language to Japanese colonisation and won legal recognition in 2019.
The Island Caribs kept their independence in the Lesser Antilles against Spain, France and England, and live today chiefly in the Kalinago Territory of Dominica.
Sailing from eastern Polynesia in waka, the Māori settled New Zealand around 1250–1350 and built a culture of iwi, pā and carved meeting houses before the Treaty of Waitangi of 1840.
Bison hunters of the northern Plains who with the Cheyenne defeated Custer at the Little Bighorn in 1876, they still refuse the 1980 Supreme Court award for the Black Hills.

title: Before the State
tagline: Cultures known from their remains, from the first settled hunters to Iron Age Europe’s walled towns.
intro: Long before writing and states, people lived in ways known only from what they left in the ground. The cultures on this path are archaeologists’ names for such remains: pottery, stone points, graves, houses and metalwork. They show hunter-gatherers making pottery in Japan around 14,500 BCE and living in permanent villages in the Levant, farmers building settlements of up to three thousand structures, herders crossing the steppe in wagons, and Iron Age communities growing rich on salt and trade. The path runs from the Jōmon to the La Tène culture, whose walled towns became Roman cities.

steps.why: For some 14,000 years the people of the Japanese archipelago lived mainly by hunting, gathering and fishing, and they made the world’s oldest known pottery around 14,500 BCE.
Hunter-gatherers of the Levant who lived in settled villages, some with round stone houses and the first known food stores, before farming began.
The earliest widely recognised culture of North America, mobile hunters of mammoth and bison with fluted stone points, though not the first people of the Americas.
Near the Bolan Pass, one of the earliest known places in South Asia where people farmed barley and wheat and herded sheep, goats and cattle.
It left the earliest known settlements on the southern Mesopotamian plain and the first temples there, but still no real cities: those came in the Uruk period.
Farmers between the Carpathians and the Dnieper who built some of the largest settlements in Eurasia, and burned and rebuilt them every 60 to 80 years.
Herders of the Pontic–Caspian steppe who moved in carts and wagons, buried their dead under mounds and are widely held to have spoken a stage of Proto-Indo-European.
Named after a drinking vessel shaped like an upside-down bell, it spread copper, gold and bronze working along sea and river routes from Portugal to Ireland and Hungary.
The salt mines of Hallstatt made its community unusually rich, and late in the period princely seats such as the Heuneburg traded with the Greek and Etruscan world.
The successor of Hallstatt from about 450 BCE, known for its curving metalwork and its walled oppida, many of which, such as Lutetia, became Roman cities.

title: The Ancient Gods
tagline: The gods of the ancient world, their temples, priests and myths, and how their worship ended.
intro: For thousands of years the peoples of the Near East and Europe honoured many gods. Every Mesopotamian city had a patron god living in its temple, Egyptian kings upheld maat, the order of the world, Greek cities held festivals and games for the Olympians, and Romans exchanged prayer and sacrifice with the gods on the principle of “I give that you might give”. Much of what is known comes from tablets, inscriptions and texts written down later by Christians. This path follows these religions from the invention of writing in Mesopotamia to the last Slavic holy places of the 14th century.

steps.why: Attested from the invention of writing around 3500 BCE, it gave every city a patron god, Marduk at Babylon and Ashur at Assur, served in a temple run as a household.
The poem of the king of Uruk and his search for immortality, one of the oldest surviving works of literature, best known from Ashurbanipal’s library at Nineveh.
For more than three thousand years Egypt worshipped Ra, Osiris, Isis and Amun to uphold maat, and its hope of eternal life inspired the pyramids and mummification.
Its pantheon of El, Asherah and the storm god Baal is known chiefly from the tablets of Ugarit, and Phoenician settlers carried it west as the Punic religion.
With no sacred book and no single priesthood, the Greeks honoured Zeus and the Olympians through sacrifice, festivals, oracles and games such as the Olympics.
Known from archaeology, often hostile Greek and Roman writers and medieval Irish and Welsh tales, it had druids, sacred groves and over two hundred named deities.
A religion of correct practice rather than belief, in which prayer, vow and sacrifice were exchanged with the gods on the principle of do ut des, “I give that you might give”.
The emperor who made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the Roman state, and the last to rule both halves of the empire before its permanent division.
The religion of Odin, Thor, Freyr and Freyja, displaced by Christianity between the 10th and 12th centuries and known mainly from Icelandic texts of the 13th.
The faith of the thunder god Perun and many-headed idols, whose rulers turned Christian between 863 and 988 while the old rites lived on in a “double faith”.

title: Faiths of the Persian World
tagline: Zarathustra’s faith, the Persian empires that kept it, and the religions that grew around them.
intro: Iran was the home of one of the world’s oldest revealed religions. Zarathustra taught a struggle between truth and the lie under the Wise Lord, Ahura Mazda, and his faith was the religion of the Achaemenid kings and the state religion of the Parthian and Sasanian empires. Under the Sasanians the prophet Mani founded a religion of light that spread from Roman North Africa to China. After the Arab conquest Zoroastrians became a minority, and some settled in Gujarat as the Parsis. This path follows these faiths and their neighbours, from the Roman cult of Mithras to the Yazidis of Lalish and the Bahá’í Faith, born in 19th-century Iran.

steps.why: The prophet whose hymns, the Gathas, stand at the origin of Zoroastrianism; his dates are disputed by a thousand years, most scholars favouring the late second millennium BCE.
Faith of the Achaemenid kings and state religion of the Parthians and Sasanians, whose ideas of judgement, heaven and hell may have influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
The Wise Lord, first notably invoked in the Behistun Inscription of Darius the Great and later named in royal inscriptions in a triad with Mithra and Anahita.
An Indo-Iranian god of covenant, truth and light, venerated in the Avesta and shown on Kushan coins, distinct from, though related to, the Mithras of Rome.
A Roman mystery cult of soldiers and merchants who met in cave-like temples; Cumont saw it as the Roman form of Persian religion, a model scholars have generally rejected since the 1970s.
A centralised Zoroastrian monarchy that ruled Iran and Mesopotamia from 224 to 651 and was Rome’s great rival for four centuries, until the Arab conquests ended it.
Founded by the prophet Mani in Sasanian Mesopotamia about 240, it taught a struggle of light and darkness and spread from Roman North Africa to China.
Descendants of Zoroastrians who left Iran after the Arab conquest, this community of western India preserved the old state faith of the Sasanian Empire.
Given its lasting form by Sheikh Adi at Lalish, the faith of the Peacock Angel remembers 74 campaigns of destruction, among them the genocide at Sinjar in 2014.
Heralded by the Báb in Shiraz in 1844 and founded by Bahá’u’lláh, it teaches the oneness of God, of religion and of humanity, and has been persecuted in Iran from its beginnings.
